cases.description: Exactly 500 operations include hundreds of close events followed by backdated financial writes and a final report.
A 101-allocation payment is rejected, then its key succeeds with exactly 100 allocations.
Valid unusual identifiers sort by ASCII; maximum-length keys and nested object reordering replay correctly.
Closing the final supported period leaves reads and historical retries available, with shape validation before close-key handling.
A failed payment key can issue an invoice; later use as a payment conflicts while reads and failed operations consume no IDs.
Undo one multi-invoice refund while a sibling refund remains active, then consume exactly the restored capacity per invoice.
Overlapping payments across three invoices retain independent refundable capacities after one refund is undone.
Refund the replacement payment in two stages until reversal of an earlier refund becomes admissible.
Corrections can post before their targets period while still open; historical prefixes exclude later invoices and closes.
Retry an older close after a later close, then attempt a correction in the intervening closed period.
Replaying the old payment and refund after both are undone and a new payment is applied cannot reactivate either event.
Nested object field order may change on retry; allocation array order remains significant after the refund is reversed.
A refund key conflicts across every other mutation kind; malformed nested input still wins before conflict and closed-period checks.
A failed refund key can reverse a payment, and a failed second-reversal key can issue an unrelated invoice.
Repeated rejected references to future event 4 become valid after successful mutations create it; reads and failures leave IDs dense.
For a reversed payment, target state wins over invalid allocation membership or capacity; closing its posting period then takes precedence.
Malformed versions of an accepted refund remain invalid even when its period is closed; the intact original still replays.
Refund and inverse sums exceed 32 bits while individual allocations stay within bounds, including historical restored balances.
A 101-entry refund fails atomically, a corrected 100-entry refund succeeds, and one reversal restores all hundred allocations.
Several reversed refunds retain separate retry identities while a later full refund remains active.
An invoice ID remains reserved after full refund and after payment reversal; its rejected duplicate key may still issue another invoice.
Refund target and posting period remain part of request identity even when allocations and monetary effects match.
Queries jump backward and forward across separate refund chains, invoice creation, closes, and reversals, then repeat an old prefix.
